messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Long-term monitoring: changing survey effort
parts:
Hi Linda:

Regarding your long-term design. Remember the two aspects to the
estimation of abundance for your marsupials: detection function and
replicate transects. I appreciate that with endangered species it is
challenging to accumulate sufficient detections to do a good job of
fitting a detection function (that was the purpose of walking transects

multiple times as you note).

On the face of it, you may not need to repeatedly walk transects, as you
propose in your new design. My concern with your proposal however, is
that you ensure you have sufficient detections within a survey window
(which you describe as occurring every year or two), so that you do not
need to pool detections across more than one or two years to fit a
detection function. As you can guess, if you need to accumulate
sightings over 3 or 4 years to fit your detection function, you need to
assume that the shape of that detection function does not change over
that period of time. The longer the time needed to accumulate
detections for fitting, the more tenuous the homogeneity of that

function becomes.

I trust you are also going to try to get even spatial coverage in your
surveys henceforth as well. So I'm afraid you need to incorporate both
adequate spatial coverage *and* sufficient detections for confident

detection function fitting into your future survey protocol.

Hope you find the advice useful.

Reinhold, Linda wrote:
> > There's a pair of islands that are inhabited by four species of endangered marsupials, which we spotlight along 40 pseudo-replicated permanent transects. It took four trips over two years to build up enough sample sizes of all of the species (each trip alone does not give enough sample sizes for discrete analyses) to get population estimates. The populations fluctuate in response to rainfall. I realise we should have done a panel design for these initial surveys to get more even coverage (the animals are more dense in some areas), but too late now.
> > Now we are "monitoring" the islands once every year or two. This is meant to be the start of an expensive long-term program which will span over decades. We are going to drop back our survey intensity to walking each transect once instead of the twice it has been the last four trips (this was to bump up the sample sizes). However, in years with more funding, we may be able to do each transect twice again. Sometimes transects are missed entirely (or only done once) anyway because we cannot access them in rough weather.
> > I'm guessing it is okay to drop back the effort to doing each transect once for long-term monitoring (from pp.75 and 107 of Advanced DS).
> > Is there then any point in doing each transect twice in those years when we happen to get lots of funding?
> > Is there anything else I need to know/change before we commit to the long-term design?

messages.author: 25f1a211d8ac38c0
messages.subject: Re: Long-term monitoring: changing survey effort
parts:
Linda,

I work with songbirds at Mississippi State University, and this question
somewhat pertains to some datasets that I am working with. Because our
sampling window for breeding season birds is limited, we often need to
pool years to increase the number of detections. I have been comparing
models with and without using year as a covariate. I checked with Eric
first and he confirmed this is an appropriate strategy. Eric stated
"The hope is that yearly variation in detectability is modelled by the
covariate, rather than being absorbed into density".

Hope this helps and thanks again Eric for your help.

function becomes.

I trust you are also going to try to get even spatial coverage in your=20
surveys henceforth as well. So I'm afraid you need to incorporate both=20
adequate spatial coverage *and* sufficient detections for confident=20

detection function fitting into your future survey protocol.

Hope you find the advice useful.
